transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I came in today because... I keep steering clear of my own workshop. And I've been avoiding any family get-togethers where my brother-in-law might be, too. Honestly, after all this time, I'm just tired of planning my whole life around making sure I don't run into those reminders. I figured it was time to finally talk to somebody about it.
Can you tell me what happened involving your workshop and your brother-in-law that made you want to start avoiding them?

Well... I'm not sure I can really get into the whole story today. I don't really know how to explain what happened, to be honest. 

It was just a really bad situation out in the shop with him a while back. I'd rather not go into the exact details of it right now, if that's alright. I just know it was bad enough that I haven't been able to step foot in that room or look him in the eye ever since.
About how long ago did that incident with your brother-in-law in the workshop happen?
Well, it's been going on since that confrontation with him... I'd say it's been about two years and four months ago now.
Since that incident, have you experienced unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about what happened, even when you're not near the workshop or your brother-in-law?

Yes, I do. Out of nowhere, I'll just... see his hand holding that heavy tool again. It's like a picture that just pops into my head. It happens when I'm just going about my day, you know, like when I'm shaving in the morning or trying to work on a painting. And even after all this time, it still makes my chest tighten up.
Since that incident two years ago, have these intrusive memories and the chest tightening been happening consistently the whole time, or have there been stretches where you didn't have them at all?

Well, I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. I mean, they've definitely been happening for a long while now, but I haven't really kept track of whether there were times they stopped completely. It just feels like it's been a constant thing in the background, you know? But as for specific stretches where it went away... I really couldn't say for certain.
Have you noticed yourself feeling unusually on edge, easily startled, or constantly on guard since the incident?

Yes, I have noticed that. I'm definitely more on guard these days. 

Like, even when I'm somewhere perfectly fine, like at the senior center or down in the church basement... I find myself constantly checking to see who just came in. I always make sure I know exactly where the door is, and... well, I keep checking whether anyone is standing too close behind me. I just can't seem to drop my guard, even when I know I'm safe.
Do you ever feel detached from yourself or your surroundings during these episodes—like you're observing yourself from outside your body, or like the world around you feels unreal or dreamlike?

No, I don't think so. I don't feel like I'm outside my body or anything like that. When those memories pop up, or when I'm checking the room... I'm definitely right there in it. It all feels very real, not like a dream at all.

Since that incident, have you noticed any lasting changes in how you feel about yourself or others—like persistent guilt, blame, negative thoughts, or a sense of being cut off or distant from people you care about?

Well, I guess... yeah, things have changed in how I look at people. I mean, I used to think family was the one place you could just relax and let your guard down. But now... I don't know, I just catch myself thinking that you really can't trust people anymore. Not even the ones who sit right there at your own table. It's just hard to look at folks the same way.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a specific traumatic event (a violent confrontation with his brother-in-law in his workshop) approximately 2 years and 4 months ago. Since then, he has experienced recurrent, involuntary intrusive memories of the event (visual flashbacks of the tool in his brother-in-law's hand) accompanied by physiological reactivity (chest tightening). He exhibits persistent hyperarousal symptoms, including hypervigilance and exaggerated need for situational awareness (checking exits, monitoring who is nearby) even in safe settings. He also demonstrates avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (avoiding the workshop and family gatherings where the brother-in-law might be present) and negative alterations in cognition/mood, specifically a persistent negative belief about trust in others ('you can't trust people anymore, not even family'). He denies dissociative symptoms (depersonalization/derealization), which argues against the dissociative subtype. Given that symptoms have persisted for over 3 months (in fact >2 years) and cause significant lifestyle restriction (avoidance behavior, social withdrawal from family events), this presentation meets criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, chronic (F43.12), rather than acute stress reaction or acute PTSD subtype.
